transcript.q: Would you like the ITIL course in-house or at a training centre?
transcript.a: In-house. The agents can be off the phones an hour at a time, at most, in quiet periods. My people can do a full day.

transcript.q: Will the provider pay half?
transcript.a: They offered to share. Nothing in writing yet.

transcript.q: Data request: Past training. I expect to see: "Who already has ITIL"
transcript.a: Provider tender response and internal training records: Provider agents on the Lysander account: 22. ITIL Foundation certified: 17. Lysander second line: 18 staff, 14 attended ITIL Foundation course in 2005, 9 passed the exam.

transcript.q: Which ITIL version do you want?
transcript.a: Version 3 came out this summer. My book is v2. With tabs. Let's do v3, it's the future.

writeup:
NEED
The reopen rate of 34% signals a gap in service maturity across the end-to-end support chain. To deliver a seamless user experience, first and second line need a shared service mindset and a common ITIL-aligned language. Learning is the lever to drive this transformation and embed a culture of service excellence at Lysander.
MEASUREMENT
We will measure success along the Kirkpatrick levels: learner satisfaction (target 4.5/5), ITIL exam pass rate (target 95%), a self-assessment of service mindset before and after, and an overall uplift in service culture and user satisfaction.
CONCEPT
A transformational, holistic learning journey based on the 70-20-10 model. The 10% is ITIL v3 Foundation with exam for all 40 first- and second-line staff. The 20% is peer learning in cross-functional communities of practice and buddy coaching between provider agents and second-line experts. The 70% is learning in the flow of work, supported by gamified microlearning on the LMS: short ITIL process bites, quizzes and badges, with a leaderboard to energise the teams. Regular lunch-and-learns and storytelling sessions keep the momentum. The journey is blended, scalable and aligned with the board's strategic priorities, and will be fully deployed before the February review.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Change management and stakeholder buy-in
- Resistance from the provider
- Keeping learners engaged
wayBack: We will monitor the KPIs and adjust where needed.

transcript.q: Do you prefer a classroom time management training or an e-learning?
transcript.a: Practical! Very concretely, something they can use Monday morning. A planning method, colour codes, priorities. I made an Excel for my own week, I can share it.

transcript.q: How many handlers can be away at once?
transcript.a: Half a day a week at most. The broker line runs 8:30 to 17:00 and must stay staffed.

transcript.q: Data request: Past training. I expect to see: "Earlier time management training and how it was rated"
transcript.a: Training records, claims department: Reorganisation 'One Customer, One Handler': information session household products, 2 hours, PowerPoint, 73 attendees. Hand-out: General policy conditions, Home Plus, 64 pages. Evaluation: none. Previous time management course (2005): 140 attendees, satisfaction 4.2/5.

transcript.q: Was the 2005 time management course appreciated?
transcript.a: 4.2 out of 5! They loved it. That was before the reorganisation of course, everyone was still in their own team then.

transcript.q: Do you feel you have too much work?
transcript.a: Too much? We have a lot, yes. Motor goes fine. Some household files are... trickier. Everyone has a little pile.

writeup:
NEED
In a fast-changing claims environment, Lindehof's handlers face mounting complexity and competing priorities. The growing backlog of 4,300 files signals a need to empower every one of the 140 claims professionals with the mindset, skillset and toolset to take ownership of their time. Learning is clearly the lever: by building strong personal effectiveness capabilities we create a culture of accountability and proactive prioritisation that will cascade into faster handling, happier brokers and fewer Ombudsman letters.
MEASUREMENT
We will apply the Kirkpatrick model at all four levels. Level 1: learner satisfaction and Net Promoter Score after each module. Level 2: knowledge checks embedded in the microlearning. Level 3: a behavioural transfer survey with the team leaders after three months. Level 4: impact on the backlog and on customer experience, with an ROI calculation to demonstrate the value of the learning investment to the board in January.
CONCEPT
A holistic blended learning journey built on the 70-20-10 model. The 10% is a kick-off workshop on prioritisation (Eisenhower matrix, the Pomodoro technique, 'eat the frog'), the 20% is peer coaching in learning circles within each portfolio team, and the 70% is on-the-job application supported by gamified microlearning on the LMS: five-minute modules, badges and a team leaderboard to drive engagement. Storytelling from top performers and a community of practice on the intranet will sustain the learning culture. The journey is designed to be learner-centric, scalable and fully aligned with Lindehof's strategic priorities, and can be live for all 140 handlers by December.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Ensuring stakeholder buy-in at all levels
- Learner engagement and time to participate
- Resistance to change
wayBack: We will continuously iterate the journey based on learner feedback.

transcript.q: Which juniors' drafts get rewritten most? Is it spread across all departments?
transcript.a: Write-offs by junior? I would have to ask finance. ... Corporate is high, yes. The recent ones. Well. Corporate documents are complex.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Write-offs concentrated in one department or intake year"
transcript.a: Time recording system, write-off report: Junior associates, drafting hours recorded vs billed, last 12 months. Firm: 24% written off. Corporate, hired autumn 2005 or later (7): 53%. Corporate, hired before 2005 (2): 13%. Tax (4): 16%. Employment (4): 14%. Litigation (5): 11%. Highest single document type: client advice memos, corporate, 61%.

transcript.q: How did juniors learn to write a memo here before 2005?
transcript.a: There was a little in-house thing, yes. Marleen's clinic. When she left I... we decided they learn by doing. As I did. It was a hundred non-billable hours a year, you understand. Tempus fugit.

transcript.q: Data request: Past training. I expect to see: "An internal memo training that stopped at some point"
transcript.a: Training file, junior associates 1999-2007: Internal training for junior associates. 1999-2005: 'Memo clinic' (M. Wuyts), 6 x 2 hours in the first three months, on the junior's own files: question, short answer, risks, recommendation. Last run: spring 2005. Not continued (decision head of corporate, June 2005). 2006: one-day seminar 'Legal writing: method and style' (external, law professor), outline: facts, applicable law, doctrine, discussion, conclusion. Rating 4.6/5.

transcript.q: What happens to a draft after a partner has corrected it?
transcript.a: They get their draft back. With comments. I write 'So what?' in the margin. Quite often. And the next draft has two more pages of case law. It is as if they think I am asking for more evidence.

transcript.q: When a draft comes back with 'So what for the client?', what do you do next?
transcript.a: Reread, add the case law I left out, restructure. I know the template, I put my research in the short answer box. Nobody ever showed me what a short answer looks like. In litigation Anne sits with her juniors for twenty minutes per draft.

transcript.q: Who could coach this, and how would the partners react if it targeted only some juniors?
transcript.a: Anne, I suppose. She has the time, litigation is slower. The partners would ask why it's only corporate. And then they would look at me. Quod erat demonstrandum.

writeup:
NEED
This is a learning problem, but not the one in the request. Rewriting is concentrated in the seven corporate juniors hired since autumn 2005: 53% of their drafting hours are written off, against 13% for the two corporate juniors hired earlier and 11 to 16% in the other departments. The firm-wide 24% hides that. These seven know the 2006 model memo and receive consistent comments ('So what for the client?'), but they were trained in academic legal method and never shown how to turn research into advice with the answer first. The memo clinic that taught exactly this stopped in 2005; Anne still does it informally in litigation, and her juniors' drafts rarely come back. They do not lack time or effort: they record 9.1 hours per advice memo against 5.2 for the others.
MEASUREMENT
Baseline: write-off rate and hours per advice memo for the seven, against the other juniors, over the last twelve months (time records), and three current memos per junior scored on a short checklist taken from the model memo (short answer that answers, risks graded, recommendation).
Behaviour: the same checklist, scored blind by a corporate partner each month on three memos per junior.
Leading: 'So what?' comments per draft; share of drafts going to the client with only minor changes.
Business: their write-offs moving toward the 11 to 16% of the others before the March evaluations, and no further corporate departures.
CONCEPT
Bring back the memo clinic for the seven: six sessions of ninety minutes between November and January, at 8:00 before the client day, on their own live files and the 2006 model memo. Anne leads, with one corporate partner co-teaching so the clinic and the corporate comments speak the same language. Each junior states the answer out loud before writing a word. Nine hours each fits inside the 50-hour non-billable allowance. No professor, no course for all 22; most of the 20,000 euro stays unspent.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Partners' meeting: they may push for a course for all 22 because it blames nobody. Geert presents it as reinstating a firm tradition that worked, with the 53% in euros against nine hours per junior.
- Anne: she won't want to be the example against her partners or lose billable time. The co-teaching corporate partner shares the stage and the finance partner credits her hours.
- Finance partner: agree beforehand that clinic hours count against the 50-hour allowance and that nobody reminds the seven of their target in January.
- The bar: no overlap, because this is advice-writing on their own files, not legal method.
wayBack: Seven juniors only, until the March evaluations. If their checklist scores have not moved and memo write-offs are still above 40% in February, we stop the clinic and take the supervision question to the partners instead.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Write-offs on junior drafting are high"
transcript.a: Time recording system, write-off report: Junior associates, drafting hours recorded vs billed, last 12 months. Firm: 24% written off. Corporate, hired autumn 2005 or later (7): 53%. Corporate, hired before 2005 (2): 13%. Tax (4): 16%. Employment (4): 14%. Litigation (5): 11%. Highest single document type: client advice memos, corporate, 61%.

transcript.q: Do you have any figures on how much the rewriting costs the firm?
transcript.a: Not on rewriting as such. Write-offs we have. A quarter of junior drafting hours, firm-wide. And a great many partner evenings.

transcript.q: Who would you like as a trainer?
transcript.a: Someone with a name. Last year's professor was rated 4.6. The partners will not pay for 'consultants', with all respect.

transcript.q: When could the juniors attend?
transcript.a: January. Before the evaluations in March. Office hours eat their target, evenings they resent. A Saturday morning, perhaps, with croissants.

transcript.q: What do you find hardest about writing for the partners?
transcript.a: Knowing what they want. They write 'So what?' and I add more analysis. Apparently that's wrong.

writeup:
NEED
- Partners rewrite too much junior work; firm-wide 24% of junior drafting hours written off
- Juniors don't structure their memos for the client
- Training is the lever: legal writing, structure, concision
MEASUREMENT
- Baseline (time records, last 12 months): write-offs per junior group. Corporate hired since 2005: 53%. Corporate before 2005: 13%. Tax 16%, employment 14%, litigation 11%. Client advice memos in corporate: 61%.
- Behaviour: before/after, three memos per junior scored blind by a partner on a checklist from the 2006 model memo (short answer, risks, recommendation).
- Business: write-off rate per group, monthly report from time records; target firm-wide below 15% by end 2008.
CONCEPT
- Two-day legal writing course in January by a well-known professor, for all 22 juniors, in their language of registration
- Day 1 structure, day 2 concision and plain language, exercises on anonymised memos
- Saturday-morning follow-up session in February
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Partners must free the juniors for two days
- Budget (20,000) may be tight for a big name

transcript.q: Since the Green Belt, how many projects did the team leads start?
transcript.a: Oh, they passed. All of them. Good scores, nice projects, nice certificates. Then nothing. That's what I mean by didn't stick.

transcript.q: Data request: Policies and targets. I expect to see: "Projects are not in the team leads' objectives"
transcript.a: HR, team lead objectives template 2007: Team lead annual objectives 2007: 1) Tonnes per shift vs. plan (50%). 2) Absenteeism of own crew (25%). 3) Lost-time accidents (25%). No other objectives.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Downtime per line and the main reasons"
transcript.a: MES downtime report, last 8 weeks: Top reason codes by minutes: Other 48%, Changeover 17%, Jam/corrugator 12%, Waiting for material 9%, Maintenance 8%, Quality hold 6%.

transcript.q: Who is supposed to give them time for projects?
transcript.a: They run around. Forklift missing, someone sick, wrong board grade. If you find one sitting down, take a photo. Project time? There's no such column on the rota. Concretely, nobody.

transcript.q: What stops you from running a project?
transcript.a: No time. Nobody asks. Line 3 changeovers went from 48 to 33 minutes on the course. Then nobody asked about it again.

writeup:
NEED
- Not a training problem: team leads passed, then 0 projects
- No time (firefighting), nobody asks, targets only tonnes/absence/accidents
- 48% of downtime coded 'Other'
- Lever: no
MEASUREMENT
- Projects opened per month (now 0)
- OEE per line, monthly
- Share of 'Other' in the MES
CONCEPT
- L&D rewrites the team lead objective template: 30% weight on project savings, replacing part of the tonnes weight. We send the new template to HR for information.
- L&D brings in an MES contractor to rebuild the reason-code tree and we retrain the operators on coding ourselves.
- L&D chairs a monthly project review with the team leads and keeps the project register.
- Refresher budget pays a floater pool managed by L&D so each team lead has 2h/week.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Works council: protected time
- HR might not agree with the new template
- Marc may not attend
wayBack: Pilot on lines 1 and 3 until end of March, then we look at the number of projects opened and decide with Marc whether to extend.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Reopens concentrated in a few categories"
transcript.a: Service desk ticket tool, reopen report: Reopened incidents, last 3 months: 1,940. Notes/Windows password sync 512, Claims application printer mapping 371, VPN token expired or not recognised 248, other 809.

transcript.q: What was the reopen rate before outsourcing?
transcript.a: Around 9%. Now 34%. Since February. The provider is ITIL-certified, it was in their pitch.

transcript.q: When do you need results?
transcript.a: A plan for the IT committee before Christmas. And the contract has a review clause in February.

transcript.q: Which tickets come back most?
transcript.a: Notes passwords. Printers in Claims. VPN tokens. Every day. We close them and they come back.

writeup:
NEED
- Reopens 9% before outsourcing, 34% now
- First and second line don't share a common way of handling incidents
- Learning is the lever: one process language for all 40
MEASUREMENT
- Baseline: reopen rate 34%, last three months 1,940 reopens of which Notes password 512, Claims printers 371, VPN tokens 248 (ticket tool)
- Behaviour: weekly sample of 20 closed tickets per team, checked for correct categorisation, resolution notes and user confirmation before closing
- Business: reopen rate below 15% by the February review; complaints in the IT mailbox
- Collection: weekly ticket tool report, sample checked by the second-line team leads
CONCEPT
- ITIL Foundation (v3) for the 22 provider agents and the 18 second-line staff, two days plus exam, in-house, provider shares the cost
- Extra half-day after the course on the three recurring problems

- Agents can only leave the phones one hour at a time
- Exam pass rate

transcript.q: Before we book anything: which flights, which aircraft and which shift were the five events on?
transcript.a: Let me pull the list... huh. All five on the Medisol 800, all before half past seven. I hadn't put them next to each other like that.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "The five events cluster on one airline, one type or one time of day"
transcript.a: Station occurrence log, September: Load discrepancies: 07/09 MSL411 B737-800 dep 06:10; 14/09 MSL415 B737-800 dep 06:40; 22/09 MSL411 B737-800 dep 06:10. Handling delays: 18/09 MSL417 B737-800 dep 07:25 (+19 min); 27/09 MSL411 B737-800 dep 06:10 (+12 min). Other airlines and cargo: 0 handling events.

transcript.q: What changed on the Medisol rotation this year?
transcript.a: Changed? Medisol went from the 300 to the 800 in May. Same airline, same suitcases, bigger plane. They mailed us a PDF with the hold drawing. Negative on anything else.

transcript.q: Who works the early shift now, and who checks the holds before the doors close?
transcript.a: Rudi ran the early shift for fifteen years. He went to cargo in August, his back. Now it's Wouter. Good kid. Two years in. And we took on nineteen for the summer and kept them for the winter charters. They did the CD-ROM and three shifts with a buddy. Same as always.

transcript.q: Data request: Past training. I expect to see: "The loading course is old and doesn't cover the 737-800"
transcript.a: Training catalogue, ramp: Loading Principles, 1 day, classroom. Last revision March 2004. Aircraft covered: B737-300, F50, MD-80. Assessment: 30 multiple-choice questions, pass mark 70%. Practical assessment: none.

transcript.q: When late bags turn up and the plan no longer fits the hold, what do you do?
transcript.a: Last-minute changes? You shift them to the back hold and close up. Who are you going to call? Load control is a number abroad, ten minutes of music. The doors close in four.

transcript.q: The Saturday trainer: is Saturday a rest day for the agents? And when can you spare people during the week?
transcript.a: Saturday is a rest day, roger. The works council will call it overtime, they always do. Between the waves I can spare a few, nine to eleven, often there's an 800 standing empty on the apron then.

writeup:
NEED
- Learning is part of the lever, not all of it.
- 5/5 September events on Medisol 737-800 departures 06:10-07:25; zero elsewhere.
- Causes: no 800 training (2004 course, no practical); 19 seasonal starters, CD-ROM only; no hold check since Rudi left; last-minute changes never reported.
MEASUREMENT
- Baseline: events per 100 Medisol 800 departures, Jul-Sep, by shift (occurrence log).
- Behaviour: hold check before doors close, sampled on an observation sheet.
- Leading: LMCs reported to load control per week (should go UP first).
- Business: Medisol events and penalty euros.
CONCEPT
- Two-hour practical on a parked 800 between waves, early shift first, real loading instruction.
- Wouter checks every 800 hold before doors close.
- Dirk agrees a quick LMC route with Medisol load control.
- Update the course later. No Saturdays.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Prevention advisor: apron safety plan before day one.
- Medisol load control: owns the LMC channel. Dirk calls them this week.
- Works council: weekday sessions, no overtime.
- Quality manager: shown sheets and LMC log, not certificates.
wayBack: Early shift only, three weeks. If observed hold checks are under 90% or there's another Medisol 800 event by week four, we stop the module and use the trainer money to bring Rudi back two mornings as a coach.

transcript.q: Where does the backlog sit, which lines?
transcript.a: By line? Let me filter... Household is 61% of the pile. And the ex-motor people take 47 days on a household file, the household people 19. Oh.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Household files are the biggest part of the backlog"
transcript.a: Claims system, open files report, end of September: Open files: 4,312. Household 61%, motor 31%, other 8%. Average days open, household files: former household handlers 19, former motor handlers 47. By peril (former household / former motor): water damage 17 / 58; storm 19 / 22; fire 20 / 21. Water damage share of household files held by former motor handlers: 71%. Average days open, motor files: 12 (all handlers).

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Household files are the biggest part of the backlog"
transcript.a: Claims intake report, monthly: New storm claims: January 2,140 (normal month: about 150). Still open from January storm: 38 (31 with loss adjuster, 7 in dispute).

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Household files are the biggest part of the backlog"
transcript.a: Claims system, monthly closing report, April to September, and HR headcount: Average days open on files closed, by month (motor / household with former household handlers / household with former motor handlers): April 21 / 33 / 49; May 23 / 35 / 52; June 18 / 27 / 50; July 12 / 19 / 48; August 12 / 18 / 47; September 12 / 19 / 47. Claims system release 2.1 deployed 18 June. Headcount claims handlers: 140 of 140 budgeted (from 136 in April).

transcript.q: What did the former motor people get as household training in January?
transcript.a: They had a presentation in January. Two hours. And everyone got the booklet. It's very complete, the booklet. Water damage is... page 31 to 38, I think.

transcript.q: What makes a household file hard for you?
transcript.a: Water. Is it a sudden leak or a slow one, do we pay the search, the plaster... In motor you wait for the expert and you know. Here nobody tells you when you know enough. Everyone has a little pile.

transcript.q: Is there budget and time for something targeted?
transcript.a: Forty thousand for the year. And they can be off the phones half a day a week, not more. The broker line stays staffed.

writeup:
NEED
- Not time management. Backlog = household water damage files with ex-motor handlers (58 vs 17 days).
- They never learned to decide cover on water (2h PowerPoint + booklet) and wait to be 100% sure, like in motor.
- Kyrill and the system are not the cause anymore.
- Training is the lever, for the ~70 ex-motor handlers only.
MEASUREMENT
- Attendance: 100% of the 70 ex-motor handlers
- Satisfaction: average 4/5 or more on the evaluation form
- End-of-course quiz on the water damage conditions (p. 31-38): 80% pass
CONCEPT
- 4 half-day case workshops on water damage cover for the ex-motor handlers, groups of 12-14
- Real anonymised files, led by a former household specialist
- Every participant gets a one-page water damage checklist
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Household specialists have no time: plan with team leaders
- Works council for half days off the phone
wayBack: We evaluate after the first workshops and adjust.

transcript.q: When do volunteers leave?
transcript.a: All the time! Some after a week, some after a year. It feels like all the time. Like a colander, I said.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Most volunteers leave early"
transcript.a: Volunteer database: Leavers in the last 12 months: 214. Left within 3 months: 146 (68%). Volunteers active more than a year: average tenure 6.5 years.

transcript.q: What does a new volunteer do in their first three months?
transcript.a: Everyone starts on the phone line. Three months. It's how Jos wanted it, so people learn to listen first. Most of them signed up to visit someone. They want a person, not a headset.

transcript.q: Data request: Process and systems. I expect to see: "A long wait before people can start"
transcript.a: Volunteer handbook, section 2: 'All new volunteers start with three months on the listening line.' Sign-up form, preferred activity: home visits 80%, phone line 12%, events 8%.

transcript.q: Data request: Process and systems. I expect to see: "A long wait before people can start"
transcript.a: Onboarding steps: Sign-up, criminal record extract request, intake interview (Thursdays, Head of Volunteering), first shift. Average days from sign-up to first shift: 43.

transcript.q: Why do people say they leave?
transcript.a: The ones who bother to tell us say 'not what I expected' or 'nobody called me'. Ouch, both.

writeup:
NEED
The coordinators are not the problem. 68% of the volunteers who leave go in the first three months, before a coordinator really knows them. Most want to visit people (80%) but have to do three months on the phone line first, after waiting 43 days to start. The exit messages say 'not what I expected' and 'nobody called me'. Learning plays a small part only; the onboarding is the main lever.
MEASUREMENT
Baseline: share of leavers who leave within three months (68%) and days from sign-up to first shift (43), both from the volunteer database. Target: under 40% and under 21 days by the end of the winter campaign. We will also track the number of volunteers who choose home visits as their first activity.
CONCEPT
Because this cannot wait for the board, the learning team will take it in hand:
- We rewrite section 2 of the volunteer handbook so that new volunteers choose their first activity, and publish the new version on the website and in the welcome pack.
- We run the intake interviews ourselves on two evenings a week to cut the waiting time.
- We call every new volunteer in their first week.
- One evening session for coordinators on welcoming new volunteers.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Jos may not like the change to the phone-line rule; we will inform him once the new handbook is out.
- Our team's time for the intakes.
wayBack: We'll see after the winter campaign whether it worked.

transcript.q: Do we need a French version?
transcript.a: One site is partly French-speaking, yes. Both languages.

writeup:
NEED
A new sepsis protocol goes live in six weeks and all 900 nurses must know it. The need is an e-learning on the protocol with a test, so the hospital can show 100% completion to the accreditation surveyors.
MEASUREMENT
- Completion rate: 100% before go-live
- Average test score of at least 80%
- Number of nurses who passed at first attempt
CONCEPT
A 30-minute e-learning on the hospital platform in Dutch and French: recognising sepsis, the screening tool, the bundle, when to escalate. Ten-question multiple choice test, pass mark 80%, unlimited retakes. Reminders by e-mail to ward heads every week until all nurses have completed.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Resistance to change
- Time constraints for the nurses
- Technical issues with the platform

transcript.q: Which leadership topics are most important for the coordinators?
transcript.a: Motivating! Recognising people. Keeping them. Some of our coordinators are fantastic, some are, how do I say, a bit chaotic. Like me.

transcript.q: When are the coordinators available?
transcript.a: Evenings and weekends mostly. Most of them are volunteers themselves. Four hours a week on average.

transcript.q: Is the 6,000 euro only for the coordinators?
transcript.a: Earmarked for 'volunteer coordinator development'. The funder is very clear on that.

transcript.q: Would you like to follow a leadership course?
transcript.a: A course? On a Saturday, I suppose. If there's soup. But honestly, the new ones mostly leave before I've even met them.

writeup:
NEED
Samen Ouder looses to many volunteers. The coordinators are the first contact person of the volunteers and they need more leadership competences to motivate and retain them. A leadership trajectory is the good answer for this and fits with the grant.
MEASUREMENT
- Satisfaction of the coordinators with the trajectory (target 8/10)
- Number of coordinators that participate (target 30 of 35)
- Total number of volunteers end of december compared to now, we want +10%
CONCEPT
Leadership trajectory of three saturdays in Mechelen with an external coach:
1. Motivation and recognition of volunteers
2. Giving feedback and difficult conversations
3. Situational leadership
Between the saturdays the coordinators make a small action plan. We foresee lunch and transport costs in the budget of 6.000 euro.
RISKS AND DEPENDENCIES
- Coordinators have little time because most are volunteer: we will foresee sandwiches and a nice location so they want to come
- Some coordinators maybe not interested
wayBack: We can always stop after the first saturday if the participants are not satisfied.

transcript.q: Do you already have a speaker in mind?
transcript.a: Navy SEAL guy, or someone like that. Last year we had a guy who climbed Everest. Incredible talk. Standing ovation.

transcript.q: Data request: Past training. I expect to see: "Last year's off-site was a success"
transcript.a: Event report, last year's off-site: Speaker 'Summit Mindset' (Everest climber). Satisfaction 9.1/10. Q1 bookings vs plan: -9%.

transcript.a: Quota attainment Q3 by cohort: Tenure > 12 months (35 reps): 94%. Tenure < 12 months (25 reps): 52%.

transcript.q: Data request: KPIs and reports. I expect to see: "Bookings down across the team"

After a tough Q3 the team needs a boost of energy and belief before the biggest quarter of the year. Learning is the lever: an inspiring off-site will reconnect the reps with their purpose and drive.
